traveler: Eustaquia de Souza & Ana de Urinza
title: Las Valientes de Potosí
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cerro Rico de Potosí, the summit
stops.campa: The mountain stands perfect as a bell over the highest city of the world, red in the morning, violet at dusk, hollowed within like a honeycomb of silver. Beneath it swarm one hundred and sixty thousand souls, more than Seville, more than London; fourteen nations of Spain quarrel in its streets and kill each other like barbarians. Kings say 'vale un Potosí' when they mean a thing beyond price. And the mountain waits, patient, for the two girls it is about to make; one day it will rise again, sun-crowned, on the first coin and the shield of a republic not yet born, Belgrano's Potosí.
suggested_refs: Gaspar Miguel de Berrío, 'Descripción del Cerro Rico e Imperial Villa de Potosí' (1758, Museo Colonial Charcas)
Primera moneda patria argentina de 1813, el Cerro con el sol (Asamblea del Año XIII)
sources: Bartolomé Arzáns de Orsúa y Vela, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí (ed. Hanke & Mendoza, 1965)
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: Bocamina on the Cerro, the mouths of the mita
stops.campa: At the mine mouths the mitayos go down by tallow-light, ladders of hide dropping into warm darkness, and come up bent under the ore that will be coined into half the money of the earth. The Villa below spends what the mountain vomits: eight fencing schools where men learn the manner of killing one another, fourteen schools of dance attended by men and women alike, gaming houses, comedias, bulls. The chronicle calls it the most splendid and the most quarrelsome town of the Indies. This is the city that eats men, and it is about to meet two doncellas it cannot eat.
suggested_refs: Anonymous, 'La Virgen del Cerro' (c. 1720, Museo Nacional de Arte, La Paz)
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí (ed. Hanke & Mendoza, 1965), t. II, las ocho casas de esgrima y catorce escuelas de danza
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: Munaypata, the two houses at the entrance of the barrio
stops.campa: At the entrance of Munaypata, where the road drops toward the ingenios of Cantumarca, stand two houses of neighbors. In one lives don Antonio de Souza, a noble Portuguese, with his son don Juan and a most beautiful little daughter, Eustaquia. In the other live don Pedro Urinza, an Andalusian knight, and his wife doña Plácida Lezama, whose only child, Ana, is a pilgrim wonder of beauty. Two girls born within a year of each other, under the same silver mountain, in the same dust of the same street. The chronicle sets down their names as if setting two blades side by side.
suggested_refs: Manuscript of Arzáns's Historia (John Carter Brown Library / Brown University copy)
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6 (ed. Hanke & Mendoza, t. II)
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: Casa de don Antonio de Souza, the orphan comes to the house
stops.campa: Doña Plácida dies while Ana is still tender, and within two years don Pedro follows her, leaving the child in the power of don Antonio de Souza, to be raised there in the company of doña Eustaquia, who at that season is likewise four years old. So the orphan of the Andalusian crosses the street and never leaves. The two girls grow as one flesh; Ana calls don Antonio and his wife father and mother, having no others. In the city of fourteen quarreling nations, one household holds a Portuguese rose and an Andalusian ember, and does not yet know what it holds.
suggested_refs: Tales of Potosí, ed. R. C. Padden, trans. F. M. López-Morillas (Brown University Press, 1975)
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6 (ed. Hanke & Mendoza, t. II)
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The estrado of the Souza house: embroidery, dance and forbidden windows
stops.campa: The girls are raised in such seclusion that neither the town nor even the barrio knows such children exist. They hear mass in the oratory of the house and enter a church scarcely ten times a year. On the estrado they are set to the almohadillas, the little embroidery cushions, and to the dances proper to doncellas. But the house has a servant boy, and he tells them of the fiestas, the comedias, the bulls, the saraos and other rejoicings of the Villa, and every word, says the chronicle, only quickens their desire to go out and see it.
suggested_refs: Arzáns on the fourteen dance schools of Potosí
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'les contaba las fiestas, comedias, toros, saraos y otros regocijos'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: Behind the door, don Juan at his fencing lesson
stops.campa: Don Antonio has his son don Juan taught to manage and play the arms of steel and of fire, and keeps weapons of every kind in the house. While the master's blade rings against the boy's, two faces watch from behind the door: Eustaquia and Ana take great pleasure in that divertimiento, and it grieves them, the chronicle says plainly, not to be men so as to wield those arms themselves. Every parry enters their eyes and is kept. The sword is learned first by stolen sight, the way saints first learn their visions: unasked, entire, and in secret.
suggested_refs: Destreza treatises of the age (Pacheco de Narváez, Libro de las grandezas de la espada)
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'les pesaba de no ser hombres para manejarlas'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The jug of water: death of don Juan de Souza
stops.campa: Don Juan is fencing with his master, sweating with the exercise, and asks for a jug of water. He drinks it, and within twenty-four hours the water has killed him: fifteen years old, the pride of his father, undone not by any blade but by a cup. The house falls into mourning; the very instrument by which don Antonio sought his son's estimation in this life becomes the origin of his greatest sorrow. Eustaquia and Ana are thirteen. The chronicle marks the hinge exactly: from this death, all their deeds descend. The brother's sword lies masterless in the house of weapons.
suggested_refs: Tales of Potosí (Brown UP, 1975), the warrior maidens episode
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'dentro de 24 horas le quitó la vida... siendo a la sazón sólo de 15 años'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The secret salle: sword, dagger, harquebus, horse
stops.campa: Fifteen months after don Juan, his mother follows him to the grave, and the girls remain alone with don Antonio. Now, whenever the father goes out, the two doncellas amuse themselves learning to fire the weapons of fire and to play the weapons of steel, thirteen years old, with more inclination to grip arms than to take up the embroidery cushions. The tradition adds that the dead boy's master, persuaded and sworn, perfects in secret what stolen sight began: sword, dagger, harquebus, and the horse. In the city of eight fencing schools, the best salle has no sign and two pupils.
suggested_refs: Badass of the Week and Rejected Princesses retellings of the secret training
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'con más inclinación a empuñar las armas... que a tomar las almohadillas'
https://www.badassoftheweek.com/ana-lezama-de-urinza
https://www.rejectedprincesses.com/princesses/the-valiant-ladies-of-potosi

stops.name: The first sally, a street of Munaypata, and Diego Melgarejo
stops.campa: By night the doncellas become caballeros. Dressed as men, armed from their father's house, they slip past the sleeping door and stop a passing youth to be their guide; he leaves what he carries and returns swiftly with a cloak and a dagger at his belt. His name is Diego Melgarejo, and he will be the secretary of all their deeds. Grateful, they tell him the truth, uncovering beautiful laughing faces and speaking in sweetest voices. Two centuries before, a maid of Domrémy put on man's iron and was believed; the crossing of dress is Joan's, and Potosí receives it.
suggested_refs: Trial records of Joan of Arc (1431), the condemnation of the man's habit
Catalina de Erauso, the Monja Alférez, who walked these same cities in men's dress
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'descubriéndose los rostros hermosos... las oyó hablar con voces dulcísimas'
Mónica Navia Antezana, 'Las damas travestidas de Charcas', Estudios Bolivianos 27 (2017)

stops.name: Plazuela de San Lorenzo, first blood, against Pimentel's ronda
stops.campa: Melgarejo leads them down the principal streets without event, until, turning home, they meet in the plazuela de San Lorenzo the servants and blacks of the justicia mayor don Luis Pimentel, who go out at night in the guise of a ronda to commit a thousand insolences, squeezing craftsmen and Indians of their goods. Steel answers insolence: a criado of the justicia mayor is left dead on the stones. The valiant doncellas set hands to swords to pursue the rest, and only Melgarejo's terror drags them home. Next day president Nestares Marín and Pimentel turn the Villa over, and can discover nothing.
suggested_refs: Portada of San Lorenzo de Carangas, the indigenous baroque gate of Potosí
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'en la plazuela de San Lorenzo se encontraron con los criados y negros del justicia mayor Pimentel'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The door at ten o'clock, víspera de San Juan
stops.campa: On Saint John's Eve at ten of the night Melgarejo waits at their door, praying to God they never come out, though he carries two pistolets now, thinking valor lives in such things. They come out. The chronicle dresses them piece by piece, armorer and lover at once: damascened cutlasses and strong bucklers, black hats, scarlet capes covered with points of silver, short skirts of silver cloth scarcely veiling the knee, doublets of blue brocade, and beneath, coats of mail. Into their guide's hands they give a most sweet vihuela, for singing in this or that street, as is the custom of the land.
suggested_refs: The chronicle's full costume inventory, alfanjes damasquinos, capas de grana, jubones de brocado azul
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'Venida, pues, la noche víspera de San Juan, a las 10 de ella...'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: Plaza del Gato, the serenade
stops.campa: Having walked some streets they come to the plaza del Gato, the market square of the fourteen nations, and seat themselves upon the stone benches as if these were the estrados of their own house. The gracious Eustaquia tunes her instrument and sweetly sings whatever she pleases, and her delicate voice and skill draw to her much of the strolling night-people of the town. Two masked caballeros, mail under brocade, playing music in the murder-streets: the city that eats men gathers round to listen, and does not know it is being serenaded by its own daughters.
suggested_refs: The vihuela and the nocturnal música callejera of colonial Charcas
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'llegaron a la plaza del Gato... cantó dulcemente lo que quiso'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The doors of the strange house, the challenge
stops.campa: Resting to play at the doors of a house where, unknown to them, doncellas live, they are accosted by four men who bid them be gone: young strangers at such doors breed suspicion. Eustaquia answers with courteous steel: they offend no one, they only rest and divert themselves with the instrument. Words sharpen. 'Be off, striplings, before we throw you off against your will.' The girls reply that now they will see whether words are equal to deeds; Eustaquia hands the vihuela to trembling Melgarejo; and Ana, drawing her pistol upon the four beards, fires: the ball parting them to crash into the doors.
stops.quote: Deteneos allá, barbados, y si no, experimentaréis la audacidad de este rayo.
stops.quote_source: Ana de Urinza, as recorded by Arzáns from the eyewitness Diego Melgarejo, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6
suggested_refs: The recorded dialogue of the challenge, preserved entire in the chronicle
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6 (ed. Hanke & Mendoza, t. II)
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The famous duel, two against four, back to back
stops.campa: Eustaquia's pistol fails fire; both draw their cutlasses and, like lions, set upon the four swords and bucklers. A point breaks through Ana's clothes and mail, wounding her below the left breast; the girl falls. Eustaquia leaps to stand over her, cutlass playing on every side, stirring her with her feet in anguish. Ana rises like a lioness, marks the man who wounded her, 'Infame, ahora me satisfaré de esta herida,' and splits his buckler and his hand. Eustaquia opens another's head to the crying-for-confession; the alférez Mendoza of Madrid lies dead; Rufino the Andalusian is maimed. She calls Ana 'don Juan' as they break away.
stops.quote: Levántate, hermana, que nos va la honra.
stops.quote_source: Eustaquia de Souza over the fallen Ana, Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6

stops.name: Cementerio de San Francisco and the arch of the bridge, the bleeding retreat
stops.campa: The barrio wakes in arms; the two break off and run. At the cemetery of San Francisco Ana can go no further, a wound in the thigh, beside the bad one in her breast, but drawing strength from weakness they reach the bridge and gather themselves beneath its arch, each binding the other's wounds, for they are bleeding out. Then down along the Ribera of the ingenios, past the sleeping silver mills, Eustaquia and Melgarejo carrying Ana in their arms because she cannot take a step. The slave opens the doors before dawn. Eustaquia bears three wounds, the one across her back perilous; Ana two, both of risk.
suggested_refs: Convento-museo de San Francisco, Potosí
La Ribera de los ingenios, the mill canal of the Villa
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'debajo del arco se recogieron a apretarse la una a la otra sus heridas'

stops.name: The sickbed and the lady of Seville, the constables baffled
stops.campa: Don Antonio, believing some other ailment, brings a physician; the girls refuse him, feigning modesty, for a doctor's hands would read the truth written on their bodies. They confide instead in a lady of Seville who lives in the neighborhood and comes visiting; she is told of the wounds and not of their cause, and God wills that she cure them rightly. Almost two months they keep their beds, and rise with all their health. Outside, the justice of two jurisdictions still hunts the two unknown swordsmen of Saint John's Eve. The constables of Potosí will never take them; the chronicle is serene on this point.
suggested_refs: The señora de Sevilla, the healer the canon leaves unnamed
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'Quiso Dios que acertase en curarlas'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The camarín window, discovery, and the rope
stops.campa: Three months healed, they summon Melgarejo for a third sally; he refuses flatly, and they resolve to walk alone. God overturns the design: don Antonio finds the men's clothes, the arms, and the pistols, and the noble Portuguese all but discharges them at his daughters. He beats them and locks them in the inner chamber, intending for nightfall a punishment that might have cost, says the chronicle, no less than their lives. But the faithful slave ties a rope to the little window of the camarín, and in nothing but their petticoats, weaponless, they drop to a stable and from the stable to the street at seven of the night.
suggested_refs: The ventanilla del camarín, the escape the canon narrates hour by hour
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'con un lazo que ató en la ventanilla del camarín las pudo ayudar a la fuga'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The house of doña Paula, refuge and the plaza purchases
stops.campa: A lady the chronicle names only as doña Paula hides them. The slave, dressed as an Indian, runs the night streets between the refuge and Melgarejo's door; the young secretary of their deeds, weighted with their money, goes into the open plaza and buys two men's suits and two swords, and it is done at once. In the richest market of the world, where anything can be had for silver, the strangest purchase of the year passes unremarked: the wardrobe of two caballeros who do not exist, paid for by two doncellas who officially never leave their father's house.
suggested_refs: The plaza and Gato market of Potosí, where everything was for sale
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'que en la plaza buscase dos vestidos de hombre y dos espadas'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: Valle de Mataca, the four mules
stops.campa: That same night, by the doncellas' disposition, a letter goes down to the warm valley of Mataca, to the slave's own son, a free black man, bidding him come with four good mules, the valiant girls sending the money to buy them. Eight days pass; then up from the valley he rides, leading four strong mules saddled and ready. He rests one day in the city of his mother's bondage. The canon gives him no name, only fidelity: he will keep these ladies' secret across five years and half a viceroyalty, and the chronicle will call him, always, el negro fiel.
suggested_refs: Río Mataca and the warm valleys southeast of the Villa
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'vino el negro hijo de la esclava con cuatro valientes mulas ensilladas'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The night road to La Plata, out of the city that ate men
stops.campa: The following night, dressed as men, the slave woman in the dress of an Indian, they thank doña Paula for the good received and ride out for the city of La Plata with the negro fiel. The lights of the Villa Imperial sink behind them; the Cerro stands black against the stars, keeping their secret with all its others. Behind, don Antonio makes every diligence, quietly, for his honor, and can find no trace of the doncellas; the sorrow of it begins to undermine and consume his health. Before them, eighteen leagues of cold road, and the world.
suggested_refs: The camino real Potosí–La Plata
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'se fueron a la ciudad de La Plata con el negro'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: La Plata (Chuquisaca), a month among the togas
stops.campa: They enter the white city of the Audiencia in their men's dress, and their beauty, says the chronicle, is a letter of recommendation: whoever sees them remains greatly affectioned, and their much discretion wins wills for them, so that they pass the month very well. Two young caballeros of no known house dine and converse under the eyes of judges who are, at that very hour, receiving dispatches about a dead alférez in Potosí and two swordsmen no constable can name. La Plata is charmed. La Plata suspects nothing. La Plata will one day hold their graves.
suggested_refs: Plaza mayor of La Plata (Sucre) and the Audiencia de Charcas
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'la hermosura de estas dos señoras era carta de recomendación'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The road down to Lima, with the merchant's train, by way of Cusco
stops.campa: At the month's end a merchant of La Plata goes down to lay out his money in Lima, and the two ride with his train: mules, silver, and a pair of doncellas whom the whole caravan takes for spirited young gentlemen. The long road of the viceroyalty unrolls: Oruro of the mines, the cold shore of Titicaca, Cusco of the Incas where two empires lie one upon the other like folded cloth. They travel as the Monja Alférez traveled it a generation before, sword at hip, sex unguessed; the road itself seems to recognize the stride.
suggested_refs: Vida y sucesos de la Monja Alférez (Catalina de Erauso), the same road in the same disguise
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'se ofreció que un mercader bajase a emplear a Lima'
Mónica Navia Antezana, 'Las damas travestidas de Charcas', Estudios Bolivianos 27 (2017)

stops.name: Lima, Ciudad de los Reyes: caballeros at the fiestas
stops.campa: In the City of the Kings, on the feast of the Kings, they shine. At every fiesta and rejoicing of the plaza they show their persons as if they really were men, the chronicle's own astonished phrase, riding, gaming, dancing at the saraos of the viceregal court: Salvatierra's now, Alba de Liste's soon. Here they win the friendship of don Juan de Itulaín, a caballero who holds them truly to be men and loves them as brothers. By day the doncellas of Potosí are the two most graceful young gentlemen in Lima; the double life has crossed an ocean of mountains intact.
suggested_refs: The Plaza Mayor of Lima under the viceroys, fiestas de plaza, cañas y toros
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'lucían sus personas como si realmente fueran hombres'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: Trujillo and the other cities, the wide circuit
stops.campa: They ride north to Trujillo of the eternal spring and to other cities the chronicle names only with a wave of its hand, and everywhere it is the same: fiestas, plazas, the flash of two matched riders whom no one doubts. The negro fiel keeps their gear and their secret; the years of the double life stretch across the whole body of the viceroyalty. Then, sated or summoned, they turn again to Lima, where the plazas keep their fiestas and the bulls their barricades, and where the long road of the double life is waiting to give the orphan its one slow wound.
suggested_refs: Trujillo del Perú in the seventeenth century
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, the circuit to Trujillo 'y otras ciudades'
Mónica Navia Antezana, 'Las damas travestidas de Charcas', Estudios Bolivianos 27 (2017)

stops.name: The bullfight, Ana on horseback, the fall in the ring
stops.campa: The plaza is barricaded for the bulls and Ana rides in among the rejoneadores, lance couched, the orphan of Munaypata running bulls before the balconies of Lima. The bull comes on; the tradition gives her the horn, the canon the fall: her horse goes down in the ring and she with it, and though she rises and finishes what she began, something in her is broken that will never wholly close. From the fall of that horse, says the chronicle exactly, was born the achaque, the long ailment. The wound of the ring enters her like a slow blade, and rides home with her.
suggested_refs: Rejoneo in the Plaza Mayor of Lima before the Plaza de Acho existed
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'se originó de la caída de un caballo en la ciudad de Lima estando corriendo unos toros'

stops.name: News from Potosí, the father's death and the testament
stops.campa: Word comes up from the mountain: don Antonio de Souza is dead, and grief finished him: el pesar lo había acabado. The father who beat them and would have punished them to death, who searched and mourned them in secret, has left a testament like a riddle of love: if his daughter Eustaquia appears, she inherits his numerous hacienda, but only if she is unmarried; married, she loses all. The old Portuguese, dying, wagers his silver that his daughter is still a doncella. In Lima two young caballeros put on mourning no one understands; nearly five years have run since the rope at the camarín window.
suggested_refs: The testament clause, herencia si no estuviese casada
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'dejó en su testamento que en pareciendo su hija Eustaquia heredase su numerosa hacienda'

stops.name: The gates of Chuquisaca, rich gowns put on at the roadside
stops.campa: At the end of five years from their going-out of Potosí, and at the twenty years of their age, they come back over the passes to Chuquisaca, the negro fiel beside them who kept the disguise with such secrecy. Before entering the city they halt at the roadside and put on their natural dress of rich gowns, with which they exalt their beauty. The men's suits are folded away, not discarded: the chronicle is precise, and the precision matters. Two ladies of fortune enter La Plata in silk. In their baggage, wrapped like relics, ride two swords and the clothes of two caballeros who have served their turn.
suggested_refs: The kept men's suits, 'tenían guardados sus vestidos de hombre'
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'se pusieron en sus naturales trajes de ricas galas'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The inheritance and the vow, toward the convento de las Mónicas
stops.campa: From La Plata, Eustaquia takes possession of her inheritance: the numerous hacienda of the Souzas, hers because she appears and appears unmarried. Then the two dispose together the last and quietest of their adventures: to become brides of Christ in the convent of the Augustinian nuns, las Mónicas. Heaven receives the intention; earth denies the habit, for the most beautiful doña Ana falls ill of that certain achaque, born of the fallen horse in the ring at Lima, and it lasts many days, and then more days. The cloister door stands open and is never passed. They nurse instead.
suggested_refs: Convento de Santa Mónica, La Plata (Sucre)
sources: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, año 1653, cap. 6, 'dispusieron entrambas el ser esposas de Cristo en el convento de Mónicas'
https://archive.org/details/historiadelavill02arzn

stops.name: The portraits, don Juan de Itulaín and the two canvases
stops.campa: Don Juan de Itulaín comes to La Plata the same year and is undeceived: his two brother-caballeros of Lima were never men. His admiration will not rest until his eyes confirm it; he begs them one day, doña Ana though sick, and Eustaquia, since they keep their men's clothes, to put them on. Importuned, they dress, and Itulaín has them painted in that costume, and at the feet of each canvas he sets the words: La valerosa doña Eustaquia de Souza; La valerosa doña Ana de Urinza, peruanas de Potosí. And they send for Diego Melgarejo, and give the secretary of their deeds a thousand pesos.

stops.name: La Plata, the death of doña Ana
stops.campa: A little more than two years in La Plata, and the achaque finishes its slow work: doña Ana de Urinza dies of the wound the ring gave her, the orphan of Munaypata, the pistol-voice of Saint John's Eve, the lioness who rose from the ground to split a buckler. At the end of her days she declares, as Eustaquia will after her, that she dies a doncella: that though they saw themselves in perilous occasions and terrible temptations, strengthening one another with the divine favor they conquered them, keeping always their chastity. Eustaquia holds the hand that held the blade at her back.

stops.name: La Plata, Eustaquia follows, of sorrow
stops.campa: Four months, no more. Doña Eustaquia de Souza dies of nothing but a corrimiento in the breast, a flowing, a defluxion, apesarada de su querida compañera, weighed down with grief for her beloved companion. The chronicle offers the physician's word and means the other one: she dies of Ana's absence, as her father died of hers. Before the end she orders all things: the great hacienda is well divided among the poor; the negra, their faithful slave of the rope and the night roads, is left free, with a quantity of silver for herself and her son, that they may live, and return to the Villa.

stops.name: The graves of the two doncellas
stops.campa: La Plata buries them as it buries its oidores, with candles and canons, and the chronicle does not trouble to name the stone, as if two who shared one childhood, one sword-master, one back-to-back night and one fortune could be expected to share one grave without its being said. Somewhere under the white city of Charcas lie the valientes, twenty-one years old forever. Their epitaph exists, but it hangs on canvas, not on stone: peruanas de Potosí. The Maid of Orléans got fire and a river; these two got portraits, and a chronicler, and the long memory of the mountain.

stops.name: Chayanta, the chronicle gathers its witnesses
stops.campa: Decades on, in the mining town of Chayanta, the chronicler Arzáns meets don Juan de Itulaín in the flesh, and hears from his own mouth the deeds of the two valorous doncellas in the City of the Kings. He has don Juan Pasquier's history, written as an eyewitness; he has three venerable elders of the Villa; he has the tales the negro fiel told Diego Melgarejo, and Melgarejo told him. One chronicle, four streams. Where the canon is a single book, the book itself shows its seams honestly, and the register takes it whole: this happened, thus, in the Villa Imperial.

stops.name: Munaypata, the clay oven of the hornero
stops.campa: The freed woman and her son ride home to the Villa with their silver, and the corpus adds the coda the chronicle only dreams: not all of the doncellas' treasure reached the poor. A remainder was sealed where no constable of any century looks: in the clay oven of the hornero, the little potter-bird, the nation's bird, who builds on lintel and post a round earthen horno that smelts nothing and hatches everything. The Cerro's silver was dead metal dug by dying men; this hoard is dead silver made living, waiting in a nest shaped like a furnace, for whoever walks the night with a sister at their back.
